SNAPCHAT / CASE STUDY
ResearchProblemDecisionFinal DesignTesting
A practice project · Snapchat

Making the rest of Snapchat easier to find.

I thought Snapchat was hard to use, so I started by looking at its menus. Then I asked people who use it. They said it was easy to get around. What they missed was friends’ Stories, Spotlight videos and Lenses. So I designed a small change to help them find those things, and left Camera and Chat as they are.

UX & UI DesignerMobile · Practice concept15 survey answers · 3 interviewsNot built or launched
01 — Overview

It started with one question.

“ Snapchat now does much more than Camera and Chat. Do people know about the rest, and does the app help them find it? ”

Role

UX & UI Designer

I did this project on my own, from the first question to the final screens. It is a practice concept. Snapchat did not ask for it, and nothing here has been built or tested.

Research

15 + 3 + reviews

A survey with 15 people, 3 interviews, and a read through App Store and Google Play reviews. It is a small group, so I use it as a guide, not as proof.

Focus

Stories · Spotlight · Lenses

Help people find what is worth opening, without slowing down Camera and Chat.

02 — Research

I talked to people before I designed anything.

I wanted to learn what people really do in Snapchat, what they know about, and how they find new things.

01 · Survey15 people answered questions about what they use, what they know about, and how they find new features.
02 · Interviews3 people who use Snapchat in different ways: someone who uses it a little or used to, someone who posts every day, and someone with a full-time job.
03 · Store reviewsI read App Store and Google Play reviews and noted the topics that kept coming up. I did not count them. They are extra support only.
10/15

opened Snapchat mainly to send a Snap or chat.

10/14

said finding their way around was fairly or very easy.

8/15

usually find new features by noticing them while using the app, not by looking for them.

12/14

rarely or never watch Spotlight, or did not know it existed.

Not everyone answered every question, so the totals are different. This is a small group I could reach. It does not speak for all Snapchat users. Most are aged 18 to 24, college students or early in their jobs, and live in Coimbatore. I sent the survey only to people who already use Snapchat, and all 15 do. I asked people I could reach and did not choose them to match a target group, so I cannot say how well they stand for Snapchat’s users, especially older people or people in other cities.

03 — Research Findings

What I learned from talking to people.

01

People open Snapchat to take Snaps and reply.

They said they open it to send a Snap or answer a friend. Nobody saw it as a place to explore. One person used Search instead of the New Chat button. A cleaner menu could have taken that habit away.

02

Content people like matters more than knowing a feature exists.

Stories and Spotlight felt less worth opening when the content did not match what people like. One person said Spotlight did not show enough of what she likes.

03

People use only a few tools.

One person mostly used Sounds and Timer. None of them used the camera AI feature. One liked Memories for looking back at old moments.

04

Sharing location is a choice.

One person keeps location sharing off on purpose, to protect their privacy. This is not a problem to fix. It is a choice the design should respect.

05

The store reviews said similar things.

The same topics kept coming up: finding things, content people like, getting around, privacy, and ads or payments. People who write reviews often write to complain, so I used them only to check that my small group was not alone.

These are my own summaries of what people said, not exact quotes. Three conversations show me what to ask next. They cannot tell me what everyone thinks.

04 — User Journey

The path I wanted to improve.

No single screen was broken. The gap was between why people open Snapchat and everything else it offers.

01 · ARRIVE

I have a reason.

I open Snapchat to chat or send a Snap.

02 · DO IT

I do it.

This part is quick and I know it well.

03 · LOOK AROUND

Is there anything else for me?

Other features need to feel useful to me, not just sit on the screen.

04 · EXPLORE

Give me a reason to look.

Content should show me why it matters now.

05 · COME BACK

Take me back to my friends.

What I find should lead back to friends and sharing.

05 — Problem Definition

The problem I decided to work on.

People open Snapchat for a clear reason and find their way around easily. What they rarely reach is friends’ Stories, Spotlight videos they like, and new Lenses.

I cannot prove this hurts people. What I can see is that they come to send Snaps and reply to friends, and Stories and Spotlight sit in places they rarely visit. Whether that is a real problem for them is the first thing I would test.

For people

Easy to miss.

Friends’ updates and content they like are easy to miss. 10 of 15 open Snapchat mainly to send a Snap or chat, 12 of 14 rarely watch Spotlight, and one person said it did not show what she likes.

For Snapchat · my assumption

Stories and Spotlight get used.

I assume Snapchat wants more people to use Stories and Spotlight. I have no Snapchat data. I use this only as a limit: I would not call it a success if people simply spend more time in the app.

06 — HMW

The question I worked on.

How can we

How can we help people find the Stories, Spotlight videos and Lenses they will enjoy, without making Snapchat more complicated?

07 — Principles & Decision

Keep what works. Fix the gap.

01 · Protect the basics

Camera and Chat are fast and people like them. I must not slow them down, and nothing I add to Chat may get in the way of replying.

02 · Say what is inside

People should know what a place is for before they tap on it.

03 · Respect people’s choices

Sometimes people choose not to use a feature. Sharing location stays optional.

A · Not chosen

Redo the whole menu

Add more tabs and reorganise the whole bottom bar. People said getting around is easy (10 of 14), so a big reshuffle could break what works.

B · Chosen

Give Explore a clear job

Fold the two places people rarely use, Stories and Spotlight (12 of 14 rarely watch Spotlight), into one clearly labelled Explore tab. The bar gets shorter, and Camera and Chat do not move.

C · Kept apart

Add groups, planning and places

These are interesting, but my research said almost nothing about them. I sketched two of them separately and did not build my case on them.

I compared these options on paper. I did not test any of them with users.

Business

Snapchat+ and ads

I removed the Snapchat+ tile from browsing because it sat among content types. Snapchat may want that upsell, so I would move it to Profile and watch whether sign-ups drop.

Success

Not just more time

I would count finding a friend’s Story or a video you like with less effort. More time in Spotlight alone does not count.

Access

Not checked yet

The “⋯” button is drawn small, and needs a tap area of at least 44 points. I have not checked contrast or screen-reader labels yet. I would before any test.

08 — Final Design

Two main stories, two smaller ideas.

Explore and Chat first. Lenses and Map after.

Explore and Chat are the two stories my research supports most. Lenses and Map are smaller ideas with thinner evidence, so I keep them short. I say so on the page. Click any picture to see it bigger.

STORY 01 · MAIN

Give Explore one clear job.

Stories are from people you know. Spotlight is from people you don’t. Today they sit side by side and the app does not explain the difference. In my design, Explore puts each kind of content in its own labelled place, so people know where to go before they tap. Then it lets friends, not just an algorithm, point people to what is worth watching.

The evidence behind it

12 of 14 people rarely watched Spotlight or did not know it existed. 8 of 15 find new features only by noticing them. One person said Spotlight did not show what she likes.

01

Four clear tabs, and one place to browse the rest.

Explore keeps only For you, Stories, Spotlight and Lenses at the top. Creators, Sounds and Games move into a Search & browse screen, grouped by type and by interest.

A long row of tabs and a category grid said the same thing twice. Now each thing has one clear place, and the Snapchat+ tile is gone from browsing.

Risk: Creators, Sounds and Games are one tap deeper. I would test if people still find them.

02

Keep friends and strangers apart.

Friends’ Stories get their own place instead of being mixed in with suggestions.

Most people open Snapchat to send a Snap or reply to a friend (10 of 15). This keeps friends’ updates from getting buried.

03

Let friends do the recommending.

Under “Liked by your friends”, each card shows who liked it, for example “Priya +2”. Only friends who chose to share their likes appear.

Interest pickers and “show less” already exist in TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, so on their own they are nothing new. Snapchat is built around real friends, so I use friends as the filter. What matches what people like then comes from people they trust. “Show less like this” stays as a small control.

Risk: I have no research showing that a friend’s taste predicts mine. That is the first thing I would test. Showing likes is also a privacy question, so nothing is shared until a person chooses Close friends, All friends or No one.

04

Find, then send.

Every pick has a send button. It opens a list of friends who share the same taste, so finding something leads straight back to a friend.

My journey ended with “take me back to my friends”. This makes it the main action, not an extra.

Risk: sending could feel like spam. I would count how many sends friends open or reply to.

05

Move Stories and Spotlight under Explore.

The bottom bar becomes Chat, Camera, Explore and Map. Camera and Chat stay where they are.

People find their way around easily, so I only touched what they rarely use. Moving a tab nobody visits costs little. It is still the riskiest choice, so I would test it first.

Risk: people used to the old tabs may look in the wrong place. If they get lost, I would keep the old tabs and add only the Explore labels.

The Explore screens, with the Stories and Spotlight screens next to them. These are ideas for making things easier to find. I have no proof yet that people find Stories faster with them.

STORY 02

Show people what they can do, right where they already are.

8 of 15 people find new features only by noticing them, and Chat is where most people already are. So I put a small “Do something together” strip in the conversation, and a sheet that opens when you want more. Chat stays as it is.

The evidence behind it

8 of 15 people find new features by noticing them. 10 of 15 open Snapchat mainly to send a Snap or chat, so Chat is where most people already are.

01

Show friends’ Stories as rings in Chat.

The Chat list has a row of story rings at the top.

Most people open Snapchat to send a Snap or reply to a friend (10 of 15). This puts friends’ Stories where they already look.

02

Suggest something to do inside the chat.

A small strip under the chat offers Try Lenses, Play a Game, Plan a place and Use this Sound. It sits below the messages, never covers them, never sends a notification, and can be hidden.

A feature appears when it is useful, so nobody has to find it by accident.

Risk: Chat is the part people like most, so the strip has one rule. If replying gets slower, it goes.

03

Keep the full list one tap away.

“Do something together” opens a sheet with Lens, Game, Plan, Sound, Memory, AI, Call, Invite and Share Profile.

The strip stays small, and everything else is still easy to reach.

SMALLER IDEA

Keep the camera fast and make Lenses easier to explore.

The camera is the habit people use most, so changing it is risky. I made Lenses a place to browse. It never gets in the way of taking a Snap.

The evidence behind it

Only 2 of 15 people had used Lens Explorer, and only 5 knew it existed. One person mostly used Sounds and Timer, and none used the camera AI feature.

Design choice

Browse Lenses in one place.

The camera still opens first. Browsing Lenses is something you choose to do. It is never in your way.

Risk: extra buttons could slow down taking a Snap. I would compare the time to the first Snap with today’s camera.

SMALLER IDEA

Make places worth visiting, and keep sharing optional.

Map is where choosing not to use a feature matters most. I designed it to be useful even when nobody shares their live location.

The evidence behind it

One person keeps location sharing off for privacy. That is only one person, so I treat it as a choice to respect, not proof that many people feel this way.

Design choice

Useful even with sharing off.

“Explore Nearby” shows places and public content to everyone. Seeing friends is a separate choice with its own Friends filter.

Risk: I do not know if people want to find places in Snapchat at all. That needs its own research.

FURTHER IDEAS

Two more ideas, kept separate.

While I worked I sketched two ideas about friends and planning. My research says nothing about them, so I am not presenting them as answers to the problem above. They would need their own research first.

Groups · no research yet

Find your people.

How could finding or starting a group feel easier in Snapchat?

Planning · no research yet

Plan together, naturally.

When a chat becomes a real plan, how could the app help without getting in the way?

09 — Testing

This is still an idea, not proof.

I have not tested any of this. Here is how I would test it, and what would make me change my mind.

Find a friend’s Story

Compare how often people succeed, how long it takes and where they go wrong, in today’s app and in my Explore design.

Find Spotlight videos they like

See if friends’ picks help people reach videos they care about, compared with the usual suggestions.

Keep Camera and Chat fast

Measure the time to the first Snap and the time to send a reply, with and without my changes. Neither may get slower.

Stop if

People already find friends’ Stories easily, or the new layout only adds confusion.

Change it if

People find the right place but misread the labels, or it takes more steps to reach Camera or Chat.

Keep testing if

People find Stories more often and Camera and Chat are not slower. Then I would test with more, and more varied, people.

Success would mean finding a friend’s Story or a video you like with less effort, not just spending more time in Spotlight.

10 — Limitations

What this study cannot tell you.

A small group.

15 survey answers and 3 interviews, mostly people aged 18 to 24 in Coimbatore (college students and early professionals). They were people I could reach, not a chosen sample, and all of them already use Snapchat. I did not hear from people who left it or never tried it. Good for finding questions, not for proving answers.

No test results.

Nobody has used these screens yet. I make no claim about speed, success or business results.

Interview notes are summaries.

They are my own words, not exact quotes.

Reviews lean negative.

People who write reviews often want to complain, so I used them only as extra support.

11 — Learnings

What I took away.

01

Don’t let your first idea become your answer.

I started by thinking Snapchat was too complicated. The research made my problem smaller, not bigger.

02

Low use does not always mean bad design.

People may not know about a feature, may not find it useful, or may choose not to use it. Each one needs a different fix.

03

Habits are a strength.

Camera and Chat are not in the way. They are what a new design should be built around.

Final thought

Keep what works.Fix the gap.

I started with “Snapchat is hard to use” and ended with a smaller, more honest question: how can people find what is worth opening without losing the quick, camera-first feel they already like?
